items.title: Israeli Authorities Trade Blame for Failure to Flag FlyDubai Co-Pilot
items.summary: The Omani co-pilot who officials said tried to crash the plane was said to have embraced extremist Islamist views.
items.full_text: The initial euphoria in Israel over the resourcefulness of passengers and crew who saved a FlyDubai flight to Tel Aviv from crashing has faded, with attention shifting sharply to the apparent security failure that almost led to a catastrophe. Amid questions about the role of the airline and the United Arab Emirates, the FlyDubai incident has also highlighted that Israel’s rules about the supervision of foreign airlines are complex and confusing — as the Israeli authorities have previously reported. Israeli government agencies on Sunday blamed one another over the seemingly inadequate vetting that allowed an Omani who was said to have embraced extreme Islamist views to co-pilot a plane from Dubai bound for Israel carrying 174 passengers, most of them Israelis. The co-pilot attacked the Indian captain of the flight on Wednesday and was trying to crash the plane before passengers and crew members intervened, with the help of the wounded captain , according to witnesses and Israeli and Emirati officials. Reserve pilots on board took over the controls and made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. An official in the United Arab Emirates said on Saturday that the co-pilot, who has been identified as Hamam al-Hammami, used an emergency crash ax in an attempt to take over the plane, adding that the attack was a terrorist operation. Mr. al-Hammami’s embrace of extreme Islamist views had prompted security officials in Oman to scrutinize him earlier, according to two people briefed on the matter . items.title: How Meta Uses A.I. Data Centers to Avoid Billions in Federal Taxes
items.summary: Meta is exploiting a lucrative tax break intended to support research and experimentation. Its own accountants say the gambit is risky.
items.full_text: Mark Zuckerberg says Meta’s A.I. push is a tremendous success. “Our investments in A.I. are accelerating every major part of our core business,” he has told investors . “Every sign that we’re seeing in our own work and across the industry gives us confidence in this investment.” But when Meta files its taxes, it tells the Internal Revenue Service a different story. It claims that its A.I. data centers are a giant experiment that could fail, according to four people with knowledge of the company’s operations. It does this so it can tap into a tax credit intended for research and experimentation. It’s an aggressive interpretation of the tax break, which Meta embraced to claim billions of dollars in tax credits for data center expansion. Characterizing its A.I. data centers as experimental is “kind of wild and out there,” said Andre Shevchuck, a partner at the advisory firm BPM who specializes in the research and experimentation tax credit. Indeed, Meta’s own accountants recognize that the strategy is on shaky legal ground. In disclosures buried in securities filings, the tech giant warns that billions in tax savings are vulnerable to being overturned by the I.R.S., in large part because of “uncertainties with our research tax credits.” Here’s what Meta is doing: For tax purposes, the company classifies its enormous, multibillion-dollar data centers as “pilot models.” Under a tax credit created in the 1980s to spur innovation, companies can get a rebate for supplies, but only if they are being tested in an experimental effort, not standard business operations. Meta is claiming that the costly A.I. computer chips it buys from companies, including Nvidia, are entitled to a taxpayer-provided discount as part of the experiment.
